# ============================================================================
# ERN research page. Edit the copy here, then rebuild:
#
#     python3 code/build_research_data.py    # only when the bibliography changes
#     quarto render research.qmd
#
# That overwrites research.html in place. git is the safety net — review
# `git diff research.html` before committing.
#
# The page chrome lives in _extensions/ern/research/template.html. Everything
# a person normally wants to change (headings, blurbs, the seven policies,
# links, footer) is a field below, so the template should rarely need touching.
#
# NOTE: values here are parsed as Markdown. Write &#39; for a straight
# apostrophe, which is what the rest of the site uses. Do not backslash-escape:
# inside a folded block scalar (>-) YAML keeps the backslash and it lands on
# the page. Colons and URLs need no escaping.
#
# The library&#39;s 162 entries are NOT in this file. They live in
# assets/data/research.json and are compiled to assets/data/research-data.js.
# ============================================================================

title: "Research and evidence on eviction — Eviction Research Network"

  author: "Eviction Research Network, UC Berkeley"
  og_title: "Research and evidence on eviction — Eviction Research Network"

  description: >-
    Seven eviction-prevention policies with measured effects, written for
    legislators and their staff, plus a searchable library of 162 publications,
    reports, and datasets on eviction, displacement, and housing precarity from
    researchers across the field.
  short_description: >-
    Seven eviction-prevention policies with measured effects, and a searchable
    library of 162 publications on eviction and displacement.
  keywords: >-
    eviction prevention policy, right to counsel, eviction diversion, rental
    assistance, just cause eviction, eviction record sealing, source of income
    discrimination, housing research, displacement, Eviction Research Network

  logo_reversed: "images/ern_logo/1Av2/EvictionStudy_logo_v09_1A_LOGO_BANNER_REV.png"

# ERN&#39;s own output. The library further down indexes the field&#39;s published
# work, four Tim Thomas papers among it, but it is not a catalogue of ERN&#39;s
# projects and datasets. Without this section the home page&#39;s "All research"
# button would land on a page that presents none of ERN&#39;s own work as such.
# These three cards are the same ones the home page carries.
ours:
  h2_lead: "From"
  h2_em: "ERN."
  sub: >-
    What we have published, built, or evaluated ourselves.
  more_label: "Read more →"
  cards:
    - kicker: "Working paper · 2026"
      title: >-
        Keeping People in Their Homes: the impact of emergency rental
        assistance on evictions
      body: >-
        A neighborhood-level evaluation of whether $46.6 billion in emergency
        rental assistance reduced eviction filings, across 700+ counties and
        12,000+ census tracts in 22 states.
      href: "https://evictionresearch.net/hud-era/"
    - kicker: "State profile · 2026"
      title: "Washington eviction filings, 2016–2026"
      body: >-
        Over the past 36 months, 1 in 45 renter households faced an eviction
        filing, roughly 49% above the pre-pandemic normal. Seven of 39 counties
        exceed the state rate.
      href: "https://evictionresearch.net/washington/"
    - kicker: "Cityscape (HUD) · 2024"
      title: >-
        Toward a national eviction data collection strategy using natural
        language processing
      body: >-
        How ERN mined 111,740 Washington court records buried in scanned PDFs
        and handwritten paper to expose the racial and gender disparities
        structured data could not see.
      href: "cityscape-2024.html"
  button:
    label: "Every state&#39;s data →"
    href: "all_states/"

brief:
  eyebrow: "Evidence brief for policymakers"
  h2_lead: "Seven policies that"
  h2_em: "reduce evictions."
  sub: >-
    Every intervention below has been evaluated in at least one U.S.
    jurisdiction and shown to reduce eviction filings, default judgments, or
    displacement. Summaries cite peer-reviewed studies and independent program
    evaluations, condensed for quick reference by legislative staff.
  primary:
    label: "Request a briefing →"
    href: "mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=Policy%20brief%20inquiry"
  secondary:
    label: "See the full evidence base →"
    href: "#library"
  policies:
    - num: "01"
      title: "Right to counsel in eviction cases"
      what: >-
        Publicly funded legal representation for low-income tenants facing
        eviction. Typically phased in by income threshold and case type.
      evidence: >-
        In New York City&#39;s pilot ZIP codes (2017–2019), 84% of represented
        tenants remained housed against roughly 30% of unrepresented tenants,
        and citywide evictions fell by 41% after universal implementation. San
        Francisco reported a 67% reduction in defaults. Similar gains are
        documented in Cleveland and Philadelphia.
      where: >-
        New York City, San Francisco, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Washington State
        (2021, statewide), Connecticut, Maryland, Minnesota, Washington D.C.,
        Boulder, Kansas City, Louisville, Toledo, Detroit.
      sources: >-
        NYC Office of Civil Justice annual reports; Stout Risius Ross (2020),
        Cost-Benefit Analysis of Right to Counsel; Seron et al. (2001),
        <em>Housing Policy Debate</em>; National Coalition for a Civil Right to
        Counsel.
    - num: "02"
      title: "Pre-filing eviction diversion and mediation"
      what: >-
        Programs that require, or strongly incentivize, landlord-tenant
        mediation before a case can be filed in court. Often paired with rental
        assistance.
      evidence: >-
        Philadelphia&#39;s Eviction Diversion Program cut filings by roughly 36%
        relative to counterfactual and resolved about half of mediated cases
        without judgment. Michigan&#39;s statewide Eviction Diversion Program
        (2020–2021) distributed $1.1 billion in rental assistance and kept about
        87% of participants housed.
      where: >-
        Philadelphia (mandatory), Michigan, Texas (Harris County), New Mexico,
        Hawaii (emergency rules), Northampton County, Pennsylvania.
      sources: >-
        Reina, Aiken, et al. (2023), Philadelphia Eviction Diversion Program
        evaluation; The Pew Charitable Trusts; National Center for State Courts.
    - num: "03"
      title: "Emergency rental assistance"
      what: >-
        Direct payment of arrears and forward rent to prevent eviction. Most
        effective when delivered within 30 days, and when landlord participation
        is structurally encouraged.
      evidence: >-
        Federal ERA1 and ERA2 ($46.5 billion, 2021–2023) disbursed aid to about
        10 million households and is credited by Treasury and the Urban
        Institute with preventing a post-moratorium eviction wave. State-level
        follow-ons in Washington, Oregon, and California show a 15% to 30%
        reduction in filings against matched controls.
      where: >-
        Washington State Eviction Rental Assistance Program, California Housing
        is Key (archived), New York ERAP, Minnesota RentHelpMN.
      sources: >-
        U.S. Treasury ERA dashboard; Urban Institute (2022), ERA Implementation
        Study; NLIHC ERA tracker; ERN&#39;s HUD-ERA evaluation with the Housing
        Initiative at Penn (2026).
    - num: "04"
      title: "Just cause eviction protections"
      what: >-
        Require landlords to cite a specific, enumerated reason (nonpayment,
        lease violation, owner move-in) before terminating a tenancy. Reduces
        no-fault displacement and retaliation.
      evidence: >-
        Oregon&#39;s SB 608 (2019), the first statewide just-cause law, was
        associated with a decline in no-cause terminations. California&#39;s AB
        1482 (2019) extended protections to roughly 9 million tenants.
        Quasi-experimental evidence from Seattle shows lower displacement rates
        for protected units.
      where: >-
        California, Oregon, Washington, New Jersey, New Hampshire, Washington
        D.C., Seattle, New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Oakland,
        Portland, and dozens of California municipalities.
      sources: >-
        Pastor, Carter and Abood (2018), USC Dornsife; Oregon Housing and
        Community Services SB 608 report; UC Berkeley Urban Displacement
        Project.
    - num: "05"
      title: "Sealing and expungement of eviction records"
      what: >-
        Automatically seal or expunge eviction filings, especially dismissed or
        settled cases, so tenants are not screened out of future housing by the
        mere existence of a filing.
      evidence: >-
        Tenant-screening companies report even dismissed filings, generating a
        mark that follows a tenant for years. Minnesota&#39;s Statute 484.014
        and Colorado&#39;s SB21-173 have reduced screening-based rejections, and
        California SB 1100 (2023) sealed dismissed filings statewide.
      where: >-
        Minnesota, Colorado, California, New York, New Jersey, Nevada, Illinois,
        Oregon, Washington. Under consideration in Arizona and Massachusetts.
      sources: >-
        Eviction Lab, The Scarlet E series; Sandefur (2014), <em>Indiana Law
        Review</em>; Kleysteuber (2007), <em>Yale Law Journal</em>; NLIHC
        eviction record sealing tracker.
    - num: "06"
      title: "Source-of-income discrimination protection"
      what: >-
        Prohibit landlords from refusing to rent to Section 8 voucher holders or
        other lawful-source recipients. Expands housing choice and reduces the
        concentration of voucher use in high-eviction neighborhoods.
      evidence: >-
        In the Urban Institute&#39;s paired-testing study (Cunningham et al.,
        2018), denial rates for voucher holders fall from 78% to 31% in
        protected jurisdictions, and voucher lease-up rates improve by 10 to 20
        percentage points.
      where: >-
        22 states and D.C., including California, Washington, Oregon,
        Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York, New Jersey, Virginia, Illinois, and
        Connecticut, plus more than 100 municipalities.
      sources: >-
        Cunningham et al. (2018), Urban Institute; NYU Furman Center; Poverty
        and Race Research Action Council source-of-income tracker; HUD PD&amp;R
        report (2022).
    - num: "07"
      title: "Extended cure and notice periods"
      what: >-
        Lengthen statutory notice-to-quit, pay-or-quit, and cure periods, for
        example from 3 days to 14. Gives tenants time to access assistance,
        rectify the default, or find counsel.
      evidence: >-
        Washington&#39;s 2019 extension of the pay-or-quit period from 3 to 14
        days, combined with standardized notice forms, was associated with a
        measurable decline in default judgments and a higher rate of tenant
        appearance in court. Similar findings in Oregon and Connecticut.
      where: >-
        Washington (14-day pay-or-quit, 2019), Oregon (10-day), Connecticut,
        Nevada, Arizona. The federal CARES Act 30-day notice remains in place
        for covered properties.
      sources: >-
        Washington State Supreme Court Gender and Justice Commission; Seattle
        University Korematsu Center, <em>Losing Home</em> (2018); Oregon Law
        Center; ERN&#39;s Washington state pipeline.
  callout:
    heading: "Why these seven"
    body: >-
      These are the policies with direct, quantified evidence of reducing
      eviction filings, default judgments, or post-filing displacement, rather
      than policies that improve tenants&#39; legal rights in the abstract.
      Complementary interventions such as rent stabilization, housing-first
      programs, and tenant opportunity-to-purchase acts also appear in the
      peer-reviewed literature, but their evidence on eviction specifically is
      more mixed or more indirect. They are covered in the library below. For a
      tailored briefing on any of the seven,
      <a href="mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=Policy%20briefing%20request">contact ERN</a>.

library:
  eyebrow: "Research library"
  h2_lead: "Everything we can find"
  h2_em: "on eviction."
  sub: >-
    Peer-reviewed publications, reports, working papers, and datasets on
    eviction, displacement, and housing precarity, from researchers, courts,
    agencies, and advocacy organizations across the field. Searchable by state,
    type, and keyword. Know of work that belongs here?
    <a href="mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=Library%20submission">Send it to us</a>.
  # Checked against assets/data/research.json by code/build_research_data.py on
  # every run. If the two disagree the script says so; fix this number, do not
  # fix the script.
  count_in_prose: 162
  search_placeholder: "Search by title, author, or publisher"
  all_states_label: "All states"
  all_types_label: "All types"
  loading_label: "Loading the library…"
  empty_label: "No publications match those filters. Try broadening the search."

contribute:
  eyebrow: "Add to the record"
  heading: "Know eviction work that is missing here?"
  body: >-
    The library is hand-maintained and it is incomplete by definition. If you
    have published research, run a court data project, or maintain a tracker we
    have not indexed, send it over and we will add it. If you need a policy
    briefing for a hearing or a bill, we write those too.
  primary:
    label: "Submit a publication →"
    href: "mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=Library%20submission"
  secondary:
    label: "See how we work →"
    href: "methodology.html"
